entities.name: Eleanor of Anjou, Queen of Sicily
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Eleanor of Anjou (died August 10, 1341) emerged as a pivotal diplomatic figure in the turbulent Mediterranean politics of the early 14th century, bridging the dynastic ambitions of the Capetian House of Anjou with the Aragonese House of Barcelona through her marriage to King Frederick III of Sicily. Born into the powerful Angevin dynasty that ruled Naples, her union in 1302 with Frederick, a former enemy, was a cornerstone of the Peace of Caltabellotta, which formally ended the War of the Sicilian Vespers (1282-1302) and reshaped the political map of Southern Italy and the wider Aragonese sphere of influence. Her role as queen consort solidified a fragile peace, enabling a period of relative stability in the Kingdom of Trinacria (Sicily) under Aragonese rule.

The marriage of Eleanor, daughter of King Charles II of Naples, to Frederick III of Sicily was a strategic rapprochement formalized by the Treaty of Caltabellotta in 1302. This agreement recognized Frederick as King of Trinacria, separate from the Angevin Kingdom of Naples, and stipulated the marriage to cement the peace. As Queen, Eleanor bore nine children, including Peter II of Sicily, who succeeded his father, thus ensuring the continuity of the Aragonese line in Sicily. Beyond her reproductive role, Eleanor actively engaged in courtly life, fostering cultural exchange and wielding influence in state affairs, particularly during her husband's frequent absences or military campaigns, demonstrating a more assertive queenly role than often acknowledged.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Eleanor of Anjou's marriage was a critical component of the Peace of Caltabellotta, ending a significant regional conflict and stabilizing the Aragonese Kingdom of Sicily for decades. Her role ensured dynastic continuity and influenced subsequent Mediterranean politics.
